### Components and relations

The heart is covered by fibrous and serous pericardial sacs.

The heart lies within the pericardium in the middle mediastinum.

The mediastinal surfaces of the left pleura and lung relate to the left anterior aspect of the aortic arch.

The heart lies behind the sternum and costal cartilages.

Spiral aorticopulmonary septum explains pulmonary trunk passing anterior, left, then posterior to ascending aorta.

Contents of the anterior mediastinum are anterior relations of the sternocostal surface.

Superior and inferior sternopericardial ligaments attach the pericardium to the sternum.

From superior to inferior, the descending thoracic aorta relates anteriorly to left principal bronchus, pericardium, esophagus, and diaphragm.

The anterior septal border corresponds to the anterior interventricular groove on the sternocostal surface.

The sternocostal surface is related anteriorly to the sternum and second through sixth costal cartilages.

The upper border is formed mainly by the left atrium and to a lesser extent by the right atrium.

A tricuspid cusp base attaches to the fibrous ring, while its free border attaches to chordae tendineae.

A papillary muscle base attaches to the ventricular wall and its apex gives rise to chordae tendineae.

Valve sounds are best heard at auscultatory areas rather than directly over anatomical valve positions because sound propagates.

### Orientation

Evidence not yet available for this section; no content was inferred.

### Components and relations

The heart has two atria and two ventricles.

The moderator band prevents overdistension of the right ventricle.

The atrioventricular bundle arises from the A-V node and traverses the fibrous skeleton to reach the interventricular septum.

The entire interventricular septum may be absent.

The aortic valve projects as a 2.5-cm oblique line behind the left sternal margin opposite the third left intercostal space.

The mitral valve projects as a 3-cm oblique line behind the left half of the sternum opposite the fourth left sternocostal junction.

The pulmonary valve projects as a 2.5-cm horizontal line behind the third left costal cartilage at the sternum.

The tricuspid valve projects as a 4-cm vertical line behind the center of the sternum opposite the fourth intercostal space.

Chordae from the anterior papillary muscle attach to the anterior and posterior tricuspid cusps.

The anterior papillary muscle is the largest right ventricular papillary muscle.

In TGA, aorta connects to right ventricle.

The aortic orifice is circular, lies horizontally at the upper aortic vestibule, and is surrounded by a fibrous ring attaching the three aortic cusps.

Three slight dilatations of the ascending aortic root opposite the cusps are called aortic sinuses.

At its beginning, the ascending aorta has three aortic sinuses opposite the aortic-valve cusps: one anterior and two posterior.

### Orientation

Evidence not yet available for this section; no content was inferred.

### Components and relations

A balanced pattern has two posterior interventricular branches, one from each coronary artery.

The small cardiac vein turns backward-left in the coronary sulcus with the right coronary artery.

The right marginal artery supplies the right ventricle.

The posterior interventricular artery gives an A-V node and bundle artery in 80% of people.

Two to four anterior cardiac veins arise from the anterior wall of the right ventricle and penetrate the anterior right atrial wall.

The ascending aorta gives the right and left coronary arteries as its two branches.

Most cardiac veins accompany arteries.

The circumflex artery accompanies the coronary sinus, with blood flowing in the same direction in both vessels.

Blockage of a coronary artery or major branch can cause myocardial infarction, defined here as death of myocardium.

Narrowing of a large coronary branch can reduce cardiac blood supply and cause myocardial ischemia.

The coronary sinus opens between the inferior vena cava and tricuspid orifices and is guarded by a rudimentary valve.

The coronary sinus runs left to right with the circumflex artery.

The anterior interventricular artery descends with the great cardiac vein to the inferior border 1.5 cm right of the apex.

The circumflex artery travels through anterior and posterior coronary sulcus and ends by anastomosing with the right coronary artery.

The heart lies within the pericardium in the middle mediastinum.
The mediastinal surfaces of the left pleura and lung relate to the left anterior aspect of the aortic arch.
The heart lies behind the sternum and costal cartilages.
Spiral aorticopulmonary septum explains pulmonary trunk passing anterior, left, then posterior to ascending aorta.
Contents of the anterior mediastinum are anterior relations of the sternocostal surface.
Superior and inferior sternopericardial ligaments attach the pericardium to the sternum.
From superior to inferior, the descending thoracic aorta relates anteriorly to left principal bronchus, pericardium, esophagus, and diaphragm.
The anterior septal border corresponds to the anterior interventricular groove on the sternocostal surface.
The sternocostal surface is related anteriorly to the sternum and second through sixth costal cartilages.
The upper border is formed mainly by the left atrium and to a lesser extent by the right atrium.
A tricuspid cusp base attaches to the fibrous ring, while its free border attaches to chordae tendineae.
A papillary muscle base attaches to the ventricular wall and its apex gives rise to chordae tendineae.
Valve sounds are best heard at auscultatory areas rather than directly over anatomical valve positions because sound propagates.
The heart has two atria and two ventricles.
The moderator band prevents overdistension of the right ventricle.
The atrioventricular bundle arises from the A-V node and traverses the fibrous skeleton to reach the interventricular septum.
The entire interventricular septum may be absent.
The aortic valve projects as a 2.5-cm oblique line behind the left sternal margin opposite the third left intercostal space.
The mitral valve projects as a 3-cm oblique line behind the left half of the sternum opposite the fourth left sternocostal junction.
The pulmonary valve projects as a 2.5-cm horizontal line behind the third left costal cartilage at the sternum.
The tricuspid valve projects as a 4-cm vertical line behind the center of the sternum opposite the fourth intercostal space.
Chordae from the anterior papillary muscle attach to the anterior and posterior tricuspid cusps.

In TGA, aorta connects to right ventricle.

At its beginning, the ascending aorta has three aortic sinuses opposite the aortic-valve cusps: one anterior and two posterior.
A balanced pattern has two posterior interventricular branches, one from each coronary artery.
The small cardiac vein turns backward-left in the coronary sulcus with the right coronary artery.
The right marginal artery supplies the right ventricle.
The posterior interventricular artery gives an A-V node and bundle artery in 80% of people.
